summary.text: The Hawaiian–Emperor seamount chain is a mostly underwater line of more than 80 volcanoes stretching about 6,200 km across the Pacific, breaking the surface in Hawaii.

In 1963 John Tuzo Wilson explained it as the work of an essentially stationary hotspot, with the Pacific plate drifting northwest over it and leaving a trail of increasingly eroded islands and seamounts.
The chain bends by about 120°, and researchers still debate whether a change in plate direction or a moving hotspot caused that bend.

facts.label: Youngest volcano
facts.value: Kamaʻehuakanaloa Seamount, southeast of the Island of Hawaiʻi

facts.label: Northernmost atoll on Earth
facts.value: Kure Atoll, in the Northwestern Hawaiian Islands

facts.label: Named after
facts.value: Many volcanoes honour former emperors of Japan

items.prompt: Picture a sheet of paper sliding slowly over a candle that stays put, leaving a line of scorch marks. If this chain formed that way, where are its oldest volcanoes?

options.label: Right beside the Island of Hawaiʻi
Scattered evenly along the whole chain
At the far northwest end of the chain
In the middle, at the bend

items.explain: The plate drifted northwest over a fixed hotspot, so volcanoes get older toward the northwest; the Emperor seamounts there are the oldest part.

items.prompt: Why does the Island of Hawaiʻi still have active volcanoes when islands far to its northwest do not?

options.label: It has more rainfall to feed the volcanoes
It sits closest to the hotspot
It lies on a different tectonic plate
It was struck by a large meteorite

items.explain: The Hawaiian archipelago is nearest the hotspot, which makes it the youngest and volcanically active part of the chain.

items.prompt: Sailing northwest from Hawaii, volcanic islands give way to atolls and finally to mountains hidden below the waves. What explains this change?

options.label: Older volcanoes went quiet, eroded and sank
Rising sea levels covered only the far islands
Coral reefs grew on top and pushed them down
Earthquakes split the far islands into pieces

items.explain: Farther from the hotspot, erosion overtook volcanic activity, leaving atolls, and the oldest volcanoes subsided below sea level as seamounts.

items.prompt: Rocks from the Emperor seamounts record that the older the seamount, the farther north it first cooled. What does this point to?

options.label: The Pacific plate has never moved
Earth's magnetic field stayed perfectly fixed
The seamounts were dragged south by ocean currents
The hotspot itself has moved over time

items.explain: A fixed hotspot would give the same ancient latitude for every sample; a north-to-south change suggests the hotspot moved in the mantle.

items.prompt: One model blames the chain's bend on a 'trench jam'. What jammed the trench?

options.label: Ice sheets pressing down on the plate
Thick, buoyant seamounts that resisted sinking
A collision with the Hawaiian islands
Lava that hardened inside the trench

items.explain: In Niu's model, the Emperor seamounts reached the northern subduction zone, resisted subduction, and so reoriented the plate's motion.

items.prompt: From near Kamchatka to just off the Island of Hawaiʻi, roughly how long is this chain?

options.label: About 62 km
About 620 km
About 6,200 km
About 62,000 km

items.explain: The chain stretches about 6,200 km (3,900 mi) and holds more than 80 identified undersea volcanoes.
